questions.stem:
Consider the following functions, where $n$ is a positive integer.

$n^{1/3}$, $\log(n)$, $\log(n!)$, $2^{\log(n)}$

Which one of the following options lists the functions in increasing order of asymptotic growth rate?

Note: Assume the base of $\log$ to be 2.

steps.title: What asymptotic growth rate means
steps.body: Function $f$ grows slower than $g$ when $f(n)/g(n) \to 0$ as $n$ becomes large. Only the large-$n$ behaviour counts, so a function that is bigger at $n = 10$ can still grow slower. The standard ladder, slowest first, is: constants, $\log n$, powers $n^c$ with small $c$, $n$, $n \log n$, higher powers, exponentials. To order four functions, rewrite each into a standard form and place it on this ladder.

steps.title: Rewrite the two unusual functions
steps.body: With base 2, $2^{\log n} = n$ because the exponential undoes the logarithm. For $\log(n!)$ use $n! = n(n-1)\cdots 1$, so $\log(n!) = \log n + \log(n-1) + \dots + \log 1$. The $n/2$ largest terms are each at least $\log(n/2)$, so the sum is at least $(n/2)\log(n/2)$. It is also at most $n \log n$. Hence $\log(n!) = \Theta(n\log n)$.

steps.title: Place the four on the ladder
steps.body: The four functions are now $n^{1/3}$, $\log n$, $n$ and $n\log n$. A logarithm grows slower than any positive power of $n$, so $\log n \prec n^{1/3}$. A power below 1 grows slower than $n$, so $n^{1/3} \prec n$. Finally $n \prec n \log n$. The ladder is $\log n, n^{1/3}, 2^{\log n}, \log(n!)$.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: This order is option (A). The quick check at $n = 2^{20}$ gives $\log n = 20$, $n^{1/3} \approx 101.6$, $2^{\log n} = 1\,048\,576$ and $\log(n!) \approx 1.9 \times 10^7$, in the same order.

shortcut.body: Rewrite first: $2^{\log n}=n$ and $\log(n!)\approx n\log n$. Now only the order of $\log n$ and $n^{1/3}$ is in doubt; the rule that a logarithm grows slower than every positive power settles it, so $\log n$ comes first. Only (A) starts with $\log n$ and ends with $\log(n!)$. Do not test small $n$: at $n=1024$, $n^{1/3}\approx 10.08$ is barely above $\log n = 10$, and below $n=2^{9}$ the order is the opposite.

traps.text: Putting $n^{1/3}$ before $\log n$ by plugging in a small $n$: at $n=16$, $n^{1/3}\approx 2.5 < 4 = \log n$. Growth rate is about large $n$, and $\log n$ is eventually below every positive power.
Placing $2^{\log n}$ last. It looks like an exponential, but with base 2 it is exactly $n$, which is far below $\log(n!) \approx n\log n$.
Treating $2^{\log n}$ as the smallest because the exponent $\log n$ is small. The exponential cancels the logarithm and leaves $n$, the second largest of the four.

recognize.clues: Four functions to be ranked "in increasing order of asymptotic growth rate", with two disguised forms: an exponential of a logarithm, $2^{\log n}$, and a logarithm of a factorial, $\log(n!)$.
recognize.contrast: This is the growth ladder, not the notation-properties rules about $O$ and $\Omega$ of sums and products: nothing here asks whether one bound implies another, only where each function sits for large $n$.

check.body: Substitute a large $n = 2^{30}$. Then $\log n = 30$, $n^{1/3} = 2^{10} = 1024$, $2^{\log n} = 2^{30} \approx 1.07\times 10^9$, and $\log(n!) \ge (n/2)\log(n/2) \approx 1.6\times 10^{10}$. The four values rise in the order the ladder gives. A small $n$ such as $16$ would put $n^{1/3}$ below $\log n$, which is why only large $n$ counts.

variation.stem: Consider the following functions, where $n$ is a positive integer: $n^{1/4}$, $\log^2 n$, $4^{\log n}$, $\log(n!)$. Which one of the following lists them in increasing order of asymptotic growth rate? Assume the base of $\log$ to be 2.
variation.explanation: Rewrite $4^{\log n} = 2^{2\log n} = n^2$ and $\log(n!) = \Theta(n\log n)$. A power of $\log n$ is below every positive power of $n$, so $\log^2 n$ comes first, then $n^{1/4}$, then $n\log n$, then $n^2$. Reading $4^{\log n}$ as $n$ gives the first option, and testing a small $n$ such as $2^{20}$ gives the second.

questions.stem: Which of the following can be recurrence relation(s) corresponding to an algorithm with time complexity $\Theta(n)$?

steps.title: What a recurrence is and how to read it
steps.body: A recurrence $T(n)=\dots$ gives the running time on input size $n$ in terms of the running time on smaller inputs plus the work done outside the recursive calls. To read its growth, picture the recursion tree: add the work at each level, then add the levels. A recurrence matches an algorithm with time $\Theta(n)$ exactly when that total is $\Theta(n)$. There are two shapes here: $T(n-1)+f(n)$ (a chain of $n$ calls) and $aT(n/b)+f(n)$ (a branching tree, solved by the master theorem).

steps.title: Option (A): chain with constant work
steps.body: $T(n)=T(n-1)+1$ unrolls to $T(n)=T(1)+(n-1)=n$. That is $\Theta(n)$, so (A) can be the recurrence of a linear algorithm such as a scan.

steps.title: Option (B): two halves with constant work
steps.body: $T(n)=2T(n/2)+1$ has $a=2$, $b=2$, so $n^{\log_b a}=n$ and $f(n)=1$ is polynomially smaller. The master theorem case 1 gives $\Theta(n)$. Unrolled: the tree has $n$ leaves and $n-1$ internal nodes, each costing 1, so $T(n)=2n-1$.

steps.title: Options (C) and (D)
steps.body: (C) $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n$: here $f(n)=n=n^{\log_2 2}$, case 2, so $\Theta(n\log n)$ (merge sort). (D) $T(n)=T(n-1)+n$ unrolls to $n+(n-1)+\dots+1=n(n+1)/2=\Theta(n^2)$. Neither is linear, so the answer is (A) and (B).

shortcut.body: Ask only how much work one level does and how many levels there are. Constant work per call and $n$ calls in total, whether chained (A) or branched (B), gives linear time. A work term of $n$ per call makes the total larger: $n$ per level over $\log n$ levels (C), or $n$ per step over $n$ steps (D).

traps.text: Rejecting (B) because the recurrence "has two recursive calls so it must be bigger than linear". The tree has $n$ leaves and each node costs 1, so the total is $2n-1$; branching only hurts when the per-node work is large.
Choosing (C): $2T(n/2)+n$ looks like (B) with a bigger term, but it is the merge sort recurrence and gives $\Theta(n\log n)$.
Choosing (D) because $T(n-1)+n$ "adds n" so looks linear. The added $n$ is paid at every one of $n$ steps, giving $\Theta(n^2)$.

recognize.clues: "Can be recurrence relation(s)" for a stated $\Theta(n)$ running time, with two divide-and-conquer shapes $aT(n/b)+f(n)$ and two chain shapes $T(n-1)+f(n)$.
recognize.contrast: The chain recurrences $T(n-1)+f(n)$ look like they belong to the master theorem but do not fit its $n/b$ form; they are unrolled into a sum instead, and only the branching ones use the three cases.

check.body: Double the input and watch the cost. At $n=1024$ the four totals are $1024$, $2047$, $11264$ and $524800$. At $n=2048$ they become $2048$, $4095$, $24576$ and $2098176$. A linear running time doubles when $n$ doubles, so only the first two behave that way; the other two grow by about $2.2$ and $4$.

questions.stem:
Consider an array $A = [10, 7, 8, 19, 41, 35, 25, 31]$. Suppose the merge sort algorithm is executed on array $A$ to sort it in increasing order. The merge sort algorithm will carry out a total of 7 merge operations.

A merge operation on sorted left array $L$ and sorted right array $R$ is said to be void if the output of the merge operation is the elements of array $L$ followed by the elements of array $R$.

The number of void merge operations among these 7 merge operations is __________. (answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: Merge sort tree for 10 7 8 19 41 35 25 31, with dashed thick boxes marking the three void merges: [8,19], [25,31] and the final merge.

steps.title: Merge sort and what makes a merge void
steps.body: Merge sort splits the array into two halves, sorts each half the same way, then merges the two sorted halves into one sorted array. For 8 elements the recursion bottoms out in 8 single elements, and the merges form a tree: 4 merges of pairs, 2 merges of four, 1 final merge, 7 in all. A merge of sorted $L$ and $R$ is void exactly when every element of $L$ is smaller than every element of $R$, that is when the largest element of $L$ is below the smallest element of $R$. Then the sorted output is just $L$ followed by $R$.

steps.title: Merges at the middle level
steps.body: $L=[7,10]$, $R=[8,19]$: $10<8$ is false, so not void; output $[7,8,10,19]$. $L=[35,41]$, $R=[25,31]$: $41<25$ is false, not void; output $[25,31,35,41]$. No void merge here.

steps.title: The final merge and the total
steps.body: $L=[7,8,10,19]$, $R=[25,31,35,41]$: $19<25$, so the output is $L$ followed by $R$ and the merge is void. Total void merges: $2+0+1=3$, which matches the picture.

shortcut.body: Write the merge tree and, at each of the 7 nodes, compare only the last element of the left block with the first of the right block. That is 7 comparisons, about one minute. No need to produce the merged outputs except to carry the blocks upward, and sorting the leaves of each subtree gives them directly.

traps.text: Answering 1 by checking only the final merge, or 7 by assuming every merge of sorted blocks is void. A merge is void only when the two blocks do not interleave.
Testing whether $L$ and $R$ are individually sorted rather than whether $\max L<\min R$. Both are always sorted in merge sort; the question is about overlap.
Answering 4 or 2 by miscounting a bottom-level pair such as $[8]$ and $[19]$, or by forgetting that the final merge is void.

recognize.clues: The question names the merge sort algorithm, its 7 merge operations on 8 elements, and a property of each merge's output that depends on the two sorted halves.
recognize.contrast: This counts a property of individual merges, unlike the usual merge sort questions on total comparisons or on the $O(n\log n)$ recurrence; here the data decide the answer, so you must trace the tree.

check.body: Replace values by ranks in the full sorted order: the array becomes $[3,1,2,4,8,7,5,6]$. A merge is void exactly when its left block holds the smaller ranks of the node. The pairs give no, yes, no, yes; the two fours give no and no; the whole array gives yes, since ranks $1$ to $4$ sit on the left. That is $2+0+1=3$ again.

questions.stem:
Consider an array $A$ of integers of size $n$. The indices of $A$ run from 1 to $n$. An algorithm is to be designed to check whether $A$ satisfies the condition given below.

$\forall i, j \in \{1, \dots, n-1\}$ such that $i > j$, $(A[i+1] - A[i]) > (A[j+1] - A[j])$

Which one of the following gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm that can be designed for the problem?

steps.title: Name the quantity being compared
steps.body: Let $d_k = A[k+1]-A[k]$ for $k=1,\dots,n-1$ be the gap between neighbours. The condition says: for any two positions $j<i$, the later gap is strictly larger than the earlier gap. So the sequence of gaps must be strictly increasing. (Arrays like this are strictly convex: they bend upward.) The question asks for the best worst-case running time to test this, so we need an algorithm and a matching lower bound.

steps.title: Reduce all pairs to neighbours
steps.body: The condition over all pairs $i>j$ looks like $\Theta(n^2)$ checks. But "greater than" is transitive: if $d_{k+1}>d_k$ for every $k$, then for any $i>j$, $d_i>d_{i-1}>\dots>d_j$. Conversely the condition on pairs includes the neighbour pairs. So the condition is equivalent to $d_{k+1}>d_k$ for $k=1,\dots,n-2$.

steps.title: Upper bound
steps.body: One pass computes each $d_k$ and compares it with the previous one: $n-2$ comparisons, $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ extra space.

steps.title: Lower bound: no algorithm can skip an element
steps.body: Suppose the array is valid (for example $A[k]=k^2$) and some algorithm never reads $A[m]$. Change $A[m]$ to a very large or very small value. For an interior $m$, $d_{m-1}$ grows and $d_m$ shrinks (or the reverse), so $d_m>d_{m-1}$ fails; for $m=1$ or $m=n$ a large enough change breaks the order at the end. The algorithm cannot tell, so it would answer wrongly. Every element must be read, so $\Omega(n)$. Together: $\Theta(n)$, option (A).

shortcut.body: Spot that the gap sequence only needs to be strictly increasing between neighbours, so one pass suffices; $\Theta(n)$ is also the floor because every element must be read. Eliminate (B) at once: an algorithm cannot beat reading the input, and a convex-array minimum search by binary search does not verify the condition.

traps.text: Choosing $\Theta(\log n)$ by analogy with binary search on a convex or sorted array. Binary search finds a point in a structure that is already guaranteed; here the structure must be verified, which needs every element.
Choosing $\Theta(n\log n)$ after thinking the pairs $i>j$ must be ordered by sorting the gaps. The gaps must already be in index order, which a single scan checks.
Choosing $\Theta(n^2)$ by testing every pair $(i,j)$ literally. Transitivity of $>$ collapses all pairs into the $n-2$ neighbour pairs.

recognize.clues: "Worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm" for a property stated over all pairs $i>j$ of an array of size $n$, where a naive double loop is the obvious reading.
recognize.contrast: Do not mistake this for a search or sorting problem that earns $\log n$ or $n\log n$: the property reduces to a neighbour check, and the lower bound comes from having to read every element.

check.body: Test the reduction on small cases. For $n=3$ the only pair is $(2,1)$, which is exactly the neighbour test. For $A=[1,2,4,7,11]$ the gaps are $1,2,3,4$, so every pair and every neighbour passes. For $A=[1,2,3,4]$ the gaps are all $1$; a pair test and a neighbour test both fail, because "greater than" is strict.

variation.stem: Consider an integer array $A$ with indices $1$ to $n$. An algorithm checks whether $\forall i, j \in \{1,\dots,n\}$ with $i<j$, $A[i]<A[j]$. Which one of the following gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm for the problem?

questions.stem:
Consider the following recurrence relations:

For all $n > 1$,

$T_1(n) = 4T_1\left(\frac{n}{2}\right) + T_2(n)$

$T_2(n) = 5T_2\left(\frac{n}{4}\right) + \Theta(\log_2 n)$

Assume that for all $n \le 1$, $T_1(n)=1$ and $T_2(n)=1$.

Which one of the following options is correct?

steps.title: The master theorem in plain words
steps.body: A recurrence $T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n)$ describes an algorithm that makes $a$ calls on inputs $b$ times smaller and does $f(n)$ extra work. Compare $f(n)$ with the leaf cost $n^{\log_b a}$ (the number of leaves of the recursion tree). If $f$ is polynomially smaller, the leaves dominate and $T=\Theta(n^{\log_b a})$. If $f$ is equal, every level costs the same and $T=\Theta(f(n)\log n)$. If $f$ is polynomially larger, the root dominates and $T=\Theta(f(n))$. "Polynomially" means by a factor $n^\varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon>0$; $\log n$ is smaller than any positive power.

steps.title: Solve $T_2$ first
steps.body: Here $a=5$, $b=4$, so the leaf cost is $n^{\log_4 5}$ with $\log_4 5=\ln 5/\ln 4\approx 1.161$. The work $\Theta(\log n)$ is polynomially smaller than $n^{1.161}$, so the leaves dominate.

steps.title: Substitute into $T_1$
steps.body: Now $T_1(n)=4T_1(n/2)+\Theta(n^{1.161})$. Here $a=4$, $b=2$, leaf cost $n^{\log_2 4}=n^2$. The work $n^{1.161}$ is polynomially smaller than $n^2$ (take $\varepsilon=0.8$), so the leaves dominate again.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: $T_1(n)=\Theta(n^2)$ is option (A). Options (C) and (D) would be the answer to $T_2$, which is only the extra work inside $T_1$.

shortcut.body: The exponents decide it: $T_2$ has exponent about $1.16$ and $T_1$'s branching exponent is $\log_2 4=2$. A smaller non-recursive term never beats a larger leaf cost, so $T_1=\Theta(n^2)$ without computing anything else.

traps.text: Choosing $n^2\log_2 n$ by treating $T_2(n)$ as if it equalled $n^2$. Case 2 needs $f(n)=\Theta(n^2)$; here $f=n^{1.161}$ is smaller.
Choosing $n^{\log_4 5}$, which is the solution of $T_2$ alone. Added into $T_1$ it is only the per-node work, and the $4T_1(n/2)$ branching gives the larger $n^2$.
Choosing $n^{\log_4 5}\log_2 n$ by multiplying the solution of $T_2$ by $\log n$, as if case 2 applied. Case 2 needs the work to equal the leaf cost $n^2$, which it does not.

recognize.clues: Two recurrences of the form $aT(n/b)+f(n)$ where the work term of the first is the second recurrence, and the asked quantity is a $\Theta$ class for $T_1$.
recognize.contrast: With a $\Theta(\log n)$ work term the case "equal to the leaves" cannot apply, unlike $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n$; keep the three cases apart by comparing exponents, not by whether $f$ looks big.

check.body: Check with sizes. Level $k$ of $T_1$'s tree has $4^k$ calls, each doing about $(n/2^k)^{1.161}$ work, so the level cost is $n^{1.161}\cdot 2^{0.839k}$, which grows by about $1.79$ per level. Costs that grow geometrically are dominated by the last level, which has $n^2$ leaves, so no $\log n$ factor appears.

questions.stem:
Consider an unordered list of $N$ distinct integers.

What is the minimum number of element comparisons required to find an integer in the list that is NOT the largest in the list?

steps.title: What is being asked
steps.body: An element comparison asks which of two list entries is larger. The task is not to find the maximum or to sort; it is only to point at any one entry that is not the largest. "Minimum number of comparisons" means the best the cleverest algorithm can guarantee in the worst case. Since the integers are distinct, exactly one is the largest, and any other entry qualifies. The list must have $N\ge 2$ entries, otherwise the only entry is the largest.

steps.title: One comparison is enough
steps.body: Compare any two entries $x$ and $y$. The smaller one has a larger entry beside it in the list, so it cannot be the largest of the list. Output it. This takes 1 comparison, whatever $N$ is.

steps.title: Zero is not enough
steps.body: With no comparison the algorithm knows nothing about order. Whichever entry it outputs, an adversary can make that entry the maximum. So at least 1 comparison is needed and the answer is 1, option (A).

shortcut.body: Think "who is certainly not the winner?": the loser of any single match. A one-line proof is the whole answer. Options with $N-1$ or more are what you pay for finding the maximum.

traps.text: Choosing $N-1$, the number of comparisons to find the maximum. The question asks for an element that is not the maximum, a much easier target.
Choosing $N$ by comparing every element with some reference. Nothing requires examining every element.
Choosing $2N-1$, a count that does not correspond to any natural algorithm for this task, perhaps recalled from min-and-max procedures.

recognize.clues: "Minimum number of element comparisons" on an unordered list of distinct integers, but the target is an entry that is NOT the largest, which is a much weaker goal than finding the maximum.
recognize.contrast: Finding the maximum needs $N-1$ comparisons, but this question asks for a much weaker goal. Read the target before applying a memorised bound.

check.body: Test it on $[5,9,2]$. Compare $5$ with $9$; the smaller, $5$, is output, and indeed $9$ is larger. For a boundary case take $N=2$, where the same single comparison works. For $N=1$ the claim fails, because the lone entry is the largest, which is why the task needs $N\ge2$.

questions.stem:
An array $A$ of length $n$ with distinct elements is said to be bitonic if there is an index $1 \le i \le n$ such that $A[1..i]$ is sorted in the non-decreasing order and $A[i+1..n]$ is sorted in the non-increasing order.

Which ONE of the following represents the best possible asymptotic bound for the worst-case number of comparisons by an algorithm that searches for an element in a bitonic array $A$?

solutionDiagram.alt: A bitonic array drawn as points that rise to a peak and then fall, with a dashed line at the peak splitting it into a rising part and a falling part, each searched by binary search.

steps.title: Bitonic array and binary search
steps.body: A bitonic array rises (strictly, since elements are distinct) up to a peak at index $i$ and then falls. Binary search on a sorted array halves the range each step by comparing the middle element with the target, so it needs $\Theta(\log n)$ comparisons. It works because one comparison tells which half cannot hold the target. The idea here is to first locate the peak, which splits the array into two sorted pieces, then search the piece that can hold the target.

steps.title: Find the peak in $O(\log n)$
steps.body: Probe a middle index $m$ and compare $A[m]$ with $A[m+1]$. If $A[m]<A[m+1]$ the array is still rising at $m$, so the peak lies right of $m$. Otherwise the peak is at $m$ or to its left. Either way half the range is discarded after one comparison.

steps.title: Search both sides, then add up
steps.body: Binary search the increasing part, and if needed the decreasing part (the same with the comparison reversed). Total: three binary searches, each $O(\log n)$, so $O(\log n)$. Lower bound: a sorted array is a bitonic array with the peak at the end, and searching a sorted array takes $\Omega(\log n)$ comparisons. Hence the best bound is $\Theta(\log n)$, option (D).

shortcut.body: Bitonic search is a few binary searches in a row, and a constant number of $\log n$ terms is still $\Theta(\log n)$. Eliminate (B) because even sorted data needs $\log n$, (A) because binary search applies to each monotone piece, and (C) because the searches are sequential, not nested.

traps.text: Choosing $\Theta(n)$ because the array is not sorted overall. Its two monotone halves can be exploited once the peak is found.
Choosing $\Theta(1)$. Even a fully sorted array needs $\Omega(\log n)$ comparisons to search, and a sorted array is a special bitonic array.
Choosing $\Theta(\log^2 n)$ by nesting a binary search for the peak inside each probe of another binary search. The three searches run one after another, not inside each other, so the costs add.

recognize.clues: A "best possible asymptotic bound" for searching, in an array that is not sorted but has a known shape: it rises and then falls, with distinct elements.
recognize.contrast: Linear search is the tempting answer for an unsorted array, but the array is not arbitrary; the shape gives two sorted pieces, so the bound is not that of plain unsorted search.

check.body: Run it on $A=[2,5,9,7,3,1]$ looking for $7$. Probe $m=3$: $A[3]=9>A[4]=7$, so the peak is at index 3 or left. Probe $m=2$: $A[2]=5<A[3]=9$, so the peak is index 3. The rising part $[2,5,9]$ lacks $7$; the falling part $[7,3,1]$ holds it. Each stage took about two probes at $n=6$.

questions.stem:
Consider the following recurrence relation:

$T(n) = 2T(n-1) + n2^n$ for $n > 0$, $T(0) = 1$.

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?

steps.title: Recurrence by substitution
steps.body: A recurrence of the form $T(n)=aT(n-1)+f(n)$ cannot use the master theorem, which handles $n/b$. The usual tool is to remove the factor $a$ by dividing by $a^n$. If $S(n)=T(n)/a^n$, then $S(n)=S(n-1)+f(n)/a^n$, a plain running sum that can be added up. Here $a=2$, so divide by $2^n$.

steps.title: Divide by $2^n$
steps.body: Divide both sides by $2^n$: $\frac{T(n)}{2^n}=\frac{T(n-1)}{2^{n-1}}+n$. With $S(n)=T(n)/2^n$ this is $S(n)=S(n-1)+n$ and $S(0)=T(0)=1$.

steps.title: Add up the series
steps.body: Unrolling, $S(n)=1+(1+2+\dots+n)=1+\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$. Multiply back by $2^n$.

steps.title: Read off the order
steps.body: The bracket is $\Theta(n^2)$, so $T(n)=\Theta(n^2 2^n)$, option (A). Check: $T(1)=2\cdot1+2=4=2(1+1)$.

shortcut.body: The non-recursive term is $n2^n$ and the recursion doubles. After dividing by $2^n$ the term becomes $n$, which is summed $n$ times, giving $n^2$. So $T=n^2 2^n$. This also explains why (B) is too small and (D) is too big.

traps.text: Choosing $n2^n$ by taking the added term as the whole answer. The term is paid again at each of the $n$ levels of the unrolling, and after scaling each level adds about $n$, so $n$ levels give $n^2$.
Choosing $(\log n)^2 2^n$, which mixes up the recurrence with a divide and conquer form $T(n/2)$. Here the argument drops by 1, not by half.
Choosing $4^n$ by multiplying the $2^n$ from the doubling by the $2^n$ in the added term. The doubling and the term interact through a sum of $n$ copies, not a product of exponentials.

recognize.clues: A recurrence $T(n)=2T(n-1)+n2^n$ with subtraction in the argument, a work term that carries the same $2^n$ as the growth, and a given $T(0)$.
recognize.contrast: Subtraction-style recurrences go to unrolling or scaling, not to the master theorem; and a work term $n2^n$ matching the growth $2^n$ is why the answer gains polynomial factors, not why it becomes $4^n$.

check.body: Test the closed form $T(n)=2^n\left(1+\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)$ against the recurrence. $T(2)=2\cdot4+2\cdot4=16$ and the formula gives $4\cdot4=16$. $T(3)=2\cdot16+3\cdot8=56$ and the formula gives $8\cdot7=56$. Both match, so the order $n^2 2^n$ is the true size.

questions.stem:
The pseudocode of a function fun() is given below (see the code block).

Let $A[0,\dots,29]$ be an array storing 30 distinct integers in descending order. The number of swap operations that will be performed, if the function fun() is called with $A[0,\dots,29]$ as argument, is __________. (Answer in integer)

solutionDiagram.alt: Bar chart of the number of swaps in each bubble sort pass for a 30-element descending array, falling from 29 in the first pass to 1 in the last, summing to 435.

steps.title: What the code does
steps.body: This is bubble sort. Each outer pass $i$ walks $j$ from 0 to $n-i-2$, compares neighbours $A[j]$ and $A[j+1]$, and swaps them when they are out of order (left larger). The largest remaining element moves to the right end each pass, so pass $i$ looks at $n-1-i$ neighbour pairs. A swap happens exactly when a pair is an inversion. The task is to count swaps for a worst-case (descending) input of $n=30$ distinct values.

steps.title: In descending order every comparison swaps
steps.body: In pass 0 the largest element sits at index 0, and each comparison finds the large element on the left, swaps it right, and meets the next smaller neighbour. So all 29 comparisons swap. After the pass the array is the original rest in descending order, followed by the maximum at the end. The same holds for the shorter passes: all comparisons swap.

steps.title: Add the passes
steps.body: Pass $i$ makes $29-i$ swaps for $i=0,\dots,28$. Total $29+28+\dots+1=\frac{29\cdot 30}{2}=435$. This equals the number of inversions of a descending array, $\binom{30}{2}$, since each swap removes exactly one inversion.

shortcut.body: Each swap of adjacent elements removes exactly one inversion, and a descending array of $n$ elements has $\binom{n}{2}$ inversions. So $\binom{30}{2}=30\cdot29/2=435$ immediately.

traps.text: Answering 465 by summing 1 to 30, adding an extra pass. The outer loop stops at $n-2$ and the last pass has one comparison, so the sum ends at 29.
Answering 870 ($30\times 29$) by forgetting the factor $1/2$ that arises because the passes get shorter, or 900 by using $n^2$.
Answering 29, the number of passes, or 30, the size of the array. The question counts swaps, and each pass makes many.

recognize.clues: Nested loops that compare and swap neighbours, run on distinct values already in descending order, with the question asking for a swap count rather than a time bound.
recognize.contrast: Counting swaps is not counting comparisons: bubble sort makes the same number of comparisons for every input, while the swaps depend on the inversions present.

check.body: Try a small descending array, $[4,3,2,1]$. The passes make 3, 2 and 1 swaps, 6 in all, and $\binom{4}{2}=6$. For $n=5$ the passes give $4+3+2+1=10=\binom{5}{2}$. The same pairs-of-positions formula, evaluated at $n=30$, must match the sum of the pass counts.

questions.stem:
Let $T(n)$ be the recurrence relation defined as follows:

$T(0) = 1$,
$T(1) = 2$, and
$T(n) = 5T(n-1) - 6T(n-2)$ for $n \ge 2$

Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

steps.title: Linear recurrences with constant coefficients
steps.body: A recurrence $T(n)=cT(n-1)+dT(n-2)$ is solved by trying $T(n)=r^n$. Substituting gives the characteristic equation $r^2=cr+d$. Each root $r$ gives a solution $r^n$, and with two different roots the general solution is $T(n)=\alpha r_1^n+\beta r_2^n$. The constants $\alpha,\beta$ are fixed by the starting values $T(0),T(1)$. The growth is that of the largest root whose constant is non-zero.

steps.title: Fit the constants
steps.body: $T(0)=\alpha+\beta=1$ and $T(1)=2\alpha+3\beta=2$. Subtracting twice the first equation from the second gives $\beta=0$, so $\alpha=1$. The $3^n$ term has coefficient zero.

steps.title: Check and answer
steps.body: $T(2)=5\cdot2-6\cdot1=4=2^2$ and $T(3)=5\cdot4-6\cdot2=8=2^3$, matching. So $T(n)=\Theta(2^n)$, option (A).

shortcut.body: Guess $T(n)=2^n$ and test it against the recurrence: $2^{n}=5\cdot2^{n-1}-6\cdot2^{n-2}$ holds because $10-6=4=2^2$ after dividing by $2^{n-2}$. It also matches $T(0)=1$ and $T(1)=2$, and the starting values fix the solution uniquely. Guessing is safe only because you verify both conditions.

traps.text: Choosing $\Theta(3^n)$ because $3$ is the larger root. The larger root dominates only when its coefficient is non-zero, and the starting values here make it exactly 0.
Choosing $\Theta(n2^n)$, the form used when the characteristic equation has a repeated root. The roots 2 and 3 are different.
Choosing $\Theta(n3^n)$ by combining both mistakes: a repeated-root form and the larger root.

recognize.clues: $T(n)$ is written from $T(n-1)$ and $T(n-2)$ with constant coefficients and two starting values, so the argument drops by a fixed step instead of dividing.
recognize.contrast: This is not a master-theorem recurrence, which needs $T(n/b)$. When the argument drops by 1 or 2, the characteristic equation is the tool.

check.body: Run the recurrence forward for a few terms: $T(2)=4$, $T(3)=8$, $T(4)=5\cdot8-6\cdot4=16$, $T(5)=5\cdot16-6\cdot8=32$. The terms exactly double each time. A surviving $3^n$ component would make the ratio of consecutive terms drift toward 3, and it does not.

questions.stem: Let $A$ be an array containing integer values. The distance of $A$ is defined as the minimum number of elements in $A$ that must be replaced with another integer so that the resulting array is sorted in non-decreasing order. The distance of the array $[2, 5, 3, 1, 4, 2, 6]$ is ___________

solutionDiagram.alt: The array 2 5 3 1 4 2 6 with the kept subsequence 2, 3, 4, 6 in thick boxes and the three replaced elements 5, 1 and 2 crossed out, giving distance 7 minus 4 equals 3.

steps.title: Restate the problem
steps.body: Replacing an element means overwriting it with any integer we like. The goal is a non-decreasing array. Elements we do not replace keep their value and position, so they must already be in non-decreasing order among themselves. The distance is the smallest number of replacements, so it equals $n$ minus the largest set of elements that can be left alone. A set of kept positions that is in non-decreasing order is a non-decreasing subsequence.

steps.title: Why the replaced values can always be filled in
steps.body: Between two kept elements $a\le b$ at positions $p<q$, the replaced positions in between can be given any integers from $a$ to $b$ in non-decreasing order, which exist because the values are unbounded integers and we may repeat $a$. Before the first kept element we can use its value, and after the last we can reuse the last value. So any non-decreasing subsequence can be kept.

steps.title: Longest non-decreasing subsequence of 2 5 3 1 4 2 6
steps.body: Let $L[i]$ be the longest such subsequence ending at index $i$: $L=[1,2,2,1,3,2,4]$. For example 6 extends the chain ending at 4, which extends the chain at 3, which extends 2, so the best is $2,3,4,6$ of length 4. No chain of length 5 exists because 5 and 1 both break the order.

steps.title: Answer
steps.body: Distance $=7-4=3$: replace $5$, $1$ and the second $2$. The array becomes $2,2,3,3,4,4,6$, which is sorted.

shortcut.body: For a 7-element array list the increasing chains by eye: start with 2, then take the smallest next values 3, 4, then 6. Check that nothing gives 5 elements. Answer $7-4$. This is safe only for short arrays; for long ones use the table $L[i]$ in $O(n^2)$ or the $O(n\log n)$ method.

traps.text: Answering 4, the length of the longest subsequence rather than the number of elements outside it.

Answering 8 by counting inversions. Inversions measure adjacent swaps, not replacements. Counting descents also gives 3 for this array, but only by coincidence, and it fails on other arrays such as 1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0 where one descent hides three replacements.
Answering 2 by replacing only the two values that look out of place, 1 and 5. After that 2, 3, 4, 2, 6 still has the second 2 out of order.

recognize.clues: The phrase 'minimum number of elements replaced' to make an array sorted, with the new integers free to choose, which asks how much of the array is already in order.
recognize.contrast: This is not an inversion count, which measures adjacent swaps. One replacement fixes an out-of-order element however far it sits from its place.

check.body: Lower bound by cases. Two replacements would leave five elements in order. Keeping the 5 limits the survivors to 2, 5, 6, which is only three. Without the 5 the rest is $2,3,1,4,2,6$, and dropping any single one of those still leaves a descent, so five cannot stay.

questions.stem: Given an integer array of size $N$, we want to check if the array is sorted (in either ascending or descending order). An algorithm solves this problem by making a single pass through the array and comparing each element of the array only with its adjacent elements. The worst-case time complexity of this algorithm is

steps.title: O, Omega and worst case
steps.body: $O(f)$ is an upper bound: the running time is at most a constant times $f$ for large $N$. $\Omega(f)$ is a lower bound: at least a constant times $f$. If both hold the time is $\Theta(f)$. The worst case of an algorithm is its running time on the most expensive input of each size, so the bounds speak about that one function of $N$. The question asks what the worst-case time of the single-pass checker is, so we find that function and bound it from both sides.

steps.title: Upper bound
steps.body: The pass compares at most $N-1$ adjacent pairs and does constant work for each. So the worst-case time is at most $c\,N$, which is $O(N)$.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: The worst input is an array that is sorted. The algorithm can stop early only when it finds a pair that breaks the order. For a sorted array no such pair exists, so it must examine all $N-1$ adjacent pairs, which is at least $N-1$ steps, hence $\Omega(N)$.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: The worst case is both $O(N)$ and $\Omega(N)$, i.e. $\Theta(N)$. Option (A).

shortcut.body: One pass over $N$ elements with a sorted input never exits early, so the worst case is exactly about $N$. A running time that is linear is both $O(N)$ and $\Omega(N)$ at once, so (A) is the only option that says both.

traps.text: Choosing O(N) but not Omega(N) because an unsorted array can stop after two comparisons. That is the best case. The worst case, which the question fixes, is the sorted input where nothing stops the scan.
Choosing Omega(N) but not O(N), perhaps believing that checking both directions needs more than one pass. A single pass can track both directions at once, so the time is at most linear.
Choosing neither: this ignores that the stated algorithm makes exactly one pass, so both bounds hold.

recognize.clues: The words 'worst-case time complexity' with both $O$ and $\Omega$ offered, for an algorithm that scans once and may stop early on a mismatch.
recognize.contrast: Best, average and worst case are different functions. Stopping early on an unsorted array describes the best case and says nothing about the worst.

check.body: Test small sizes on a sorted array. $N=2$ needs 1 comparison, $N=3$ needs 2, $N=4$ needs 3, so each added element adds one comparison. Doubling $N$ roughly doubles the work, which a super-linear lower bound could not allow and a sub-linear upper bound could not match.

questions.stem:
Consider the following recurrence relation:

$T(n) = \begin{cases} \sqrt{n}\,T(\sqrt{n}) + n & \text{for } n \ge 1,\\ 1 & \text{for } n = 1.\end{cases}$

Which one of the following options is CORRECT?

steps.title: What is unusual here
steps.body: The master theorem needs the input to shrink by a constant factor, $n/b$. Here it shrinks to $\sqrt n$, much faster, and the multiplier of the recursive call is $\sqrt n$ rather than a constant. The tool for this kind of recurrence is a change of variable that turns it into a simpler one, and often dividing by the multiplier to turn the multiplier into 1. We use both: first divide by $n$, then count how many times we can take square roots.

steps.title: Divide by $n$
steps.body: Let $S(n)=T(n)/n$. Dividing the recurrence by $n$ and using $\sqrt n\cdot T(\sqrt n)/n = T(\sqrt n)/\sqrt n = S(\sqrt n)$ gives $S(n)=S(\sqrt n)+1$ with $S(1)=1$.

steps.title: Count the square roots
steps.body: Each step replaces $n$ by $\sqrt n$ and adds 1. Start with $n=2^{2^k}$: after $j$ steps the argument is $2^{2^{k-j}}$, reaching $2$ after exactly $k$ steps. Past that point only a constant number of base-case terms remain, so $S(n)=k+O(1)=\Theta(k)$ with $k=\log_2\log_2 n$.

steps.title: Multiply back
steps.body: $T(n)=n\,S(n)=\Theta(n\log\log n)$, option (A). Numerically, taking $T(n)=1$ for $n\le 2$ as the base, for $n=2^{2^k}$ the ratio $T(n)/n$ equals $k+0.5$ ($1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5$ for $k=1..4$), growing like $k=\log\log n$.

shortcut.body: Divide by $n$ at once: the recurrence becomes "add 1 each time the input is square-rooted". The number of square roots until you reach 1 is $\log\log n$, so $T=n\log\log n$. Options with $n^2$ cannot be right because the work at the top is only $n$ and the recursive part is about the same size as it.

traps.text: Choosing $n\log n$, the answer for $2T(n/2)+n$. Here the input is square-rooted, not halved, so the number of levels is $\log\log n$, not $\log n$.
Choosing $n^2\log n$ by reading $\sqrt n\,T(\sqrt n)$ as if it had a multiplier large enough to square the total. The multiplier times the subproblem size is $\sqrt n\cdot\sqrt n=n$ at most.
Choosing $n^2\log\log n$, which has the correct number of levels but an $n^2$ per level that nothing in the recurrence produces.

recognize.clues: A square root of $n$ inside $T$ together with a $\sqrt n$ multiplier, so the input does not shrink by a constant factor and no $T(n/b)$ form is present.
recognize.contrast: Compare $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n$: halving gives $\log n$ levels, but square-rooting gives only $\log\log n$ levels. Count the levels before choosing the shape of the answer.

check.body: Unroll two levels by hand. $T(n)=\sqrt n\,T(\sqrt n)+n=\sqrt n\,(n^{1/4}T(n^{1/4})+\sqrt n)+n=n^{3/4}T(n^{1/4})+2n$. Two levels cost $2n$ in total, so every level contributes $n$, and the number of levels sets the factor in front of $n$.

questions.stem:
Let $f$ and $g$ be functions of natural numbers given by $f(n) = n$ and $g(n) = n^2$.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

steps.title: The four notations
steps.body: For functions of $n$: $f\in O(g)$ means $f$ is at most a constant times $g$ for large $n$ (an upper bound, possibly tight). $f\in\Omega(g)$ means $f$ is at least a constant times $g$ (a lower bound). $f\in o(g)$ means $f/g\to0$, so $f$ is strictly smaller in growth. $f\in\Theta(g)$ means both $O$ and $\Omega$, the same growth. The quickest test is the limit of $f/g$: 0 means $O$ and $o$; a positive constant means $\Theta$; infinity means $\Omega$ without $O$.

steps.title: Compute the limit
steps.body: $f(n)/g(n)=n/n^2=1/n\to0$ as $n\to\infty$.

steps.title: Check each statement
steps.body: (A) $f\in O(g)$: true, since $n\le n^2$ for $n\ge1$. (B) $f\in\Omega(g)$: false, since $n\ge c\,n^2$ fails for large $n$ for every $c>0$. (C) $f\in o(g)$: true, the limit is 0. (D) $f\in\Theta(g)$: false, it needs (B). Answer: (A) and (C).

shortcut.body: One limit, $n/n^2\to0$: $f$ is strictly slower than $g$, so $O$ and $o$ hold and $\Omega$ and $\Theta$ do not. A 20-second answer.

traps.text: Leaving out (C). A limit of 0 gives both $O$ and the stronger $o$, so a candidate who knows only $O$ ticks one box and loses the question; MSQ has no partial marks.
Ticking (B) after mixing up the direction: $f\in\Omega(g)$ means $f$ is at least $g$ in growth, and $n$ is not at least $n^2$.
Ticking (D) because both are polynomials. $\Theta$ needs the same degree.

recognize.clues: Two plain power functions compared with $O$, $\Omega$, $o$ and $\Theta$ in a select-all-that-apply format.
recognize.contrast: Small $o$ is stronger than big $O$: a ratio that tends to 0 satisfies both, while a bounded non-zero ratio satisfies only $O$. Test both whenever the ratio vanishes.

check.body: Check against the definitions with numbers. For the upper bound, $n\le 1\cdot n^2$ holds from $n=1$. For a lower bound with the tiny constant $c=0.001$, $n\ge c\,n^2$ fails once $n>1000$, and any positive $c$ fails eventually. At $n=10^6$ the ratio is $10^{-6}$.

questions.stem:
Consider functions Function 1 and Function 2 expressed in pseudocode as follows (see the code block).

Let $f_1(n)$ and $f_2(n)$ denote the number of times the statement "x = x + 1" is executed in Function 1 and Function 2, respectively.

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

code.text:
Function 1
while n > 1 do
    for i = 1 to n do
        x = x + 1;
    end for
    n = n/2;
end while

Function 2
for i = 1 to 100 * n do
    x = x + 1;
end for

steps.title: Count the executions
steps.body: The statement count is the running time we compare. Function 2 is a single loop of $100n$ iterations, so $f_2(n)=100n$. Function 1 has a while loop in which $n$ is halved each round, and in each round the inner loop runs the current $n$ times. So the count is $n+n/2+n/4+\dots$, down to 2 (the loop stops when $n\le1$). For a power of 2, $n=2^k$, it is $2^k+2^{k-1}+\dots+2=2n-2$.

steps.title: The notations
steps.body: $f\in\Theta(g)$: same growth up to constants. $f\in o(g)$: $f/g\to0$. $f\in\omega(g)$: $f/g\to\infty$. $f\in O(g)$: $f/g$ stays bounded. Take the ratio and see which of these it satisfies.

steps.title: Decide each statement
steps.body: The ratio tends to the positive constant $1/50$. (A) $f_1\in\Theta(f_2)$: true. (B) $f_1\in o(f_2)$: false, the ratio does not go to 0. (C) $f_1\in\omega(f_2)$: false, the ratio does not go to $\infty$. (D) $f_1\in O(n)$: true, $f_1\approx2n$. Answer: (A) and (D).

shortcut.body: Function 1 is the geometric series $n+n/2+\dots\le2n$, so it is linear, and Function 2 is $100n$, also linear. Same order, so (A) is true and both $o$ and $\omega$ are false. Since $f_1$ is linear, (D) is true. Constants like 100 never change the order.

traps.text: Taking Function 1 as $n\log n$ because it has a loop inside a loop that halves. The inner loop shrinks each round, so the sum is geometric, about $2n$, not $n$ per round for $\log n$ rounds.
Ticking (B) because $100n$ "looks bigger" than $2n$. A constant factor of 50 does not make the ratio go to 0, so $o$ is false.
Ticking (C) after taking Function 1 as $n\log n$, which would be $\omega(n)$. With the correct count it is not.
Leaving out (D): the question asks about $O(n)$, not about $f_2$, and the correct count $2n-2$ is linear.

recognize.clues: Two code fragments whose statement counts must be found first, one a halving while loop that holds a full inner loop, then compared with $\Theta$, $o$, $\omega$ and $O$.
recognize.contrast: A loop inside a loop is not automatically quadratic or $n\log n$. Ask whether the inner bound shrinks with the outer variable; here it does, so the sum is geometric.

check.body: Count for $n=16$ by hand. Function 1 runs inner loops of length $16,8,4,2$, which is $30=2n-2$ executions. Function 2 runs $100\cdot16=1600$. The ratio $30/1600\approx 0.019$ is near $1/50$, and $(2n-2)/(100n)$ tends to $0.02$ as $n$ grows.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements is TRUE for all positive functions $f(n)$?
options: $f(n^2) = O(f(n)^2)$, when $f(n)$ is an exponential function

steps.title: The comparison words and the one ratio that decides them
steps.body: Asymptotic notation compares two functions for large $n$ only. For a function $g$: $f=O(g)$ means $f(n)\le c\,g(n)$ for some constant $c>0$ and all large $n$, so $f$ is not above $g$. $f=\Omega(g)$ means $f(n)\ge c\,g(n)$, so $f$ is not below $g$. $f=\Theta(g)$ means both, so the ratio $f/g$ stays between two positive constants. $f=o(g)$ means $f/g\to0$, so $f$ is strictly smaller. Here the right side is $g(n)=f(n)^2$, the square of the value $f(n)$, while the left side $f(n^2)$ puts $n^2$ into $f$; these are different things. The question says "TRUE for all positive functions", so an option is dead as soon as one positive function breaks it. Options (A) and (C) narrow the claim to polynomials and exponentials, so test them only inside that family. The ratio to watch is the one below.

steps.title: Option (A): polynomials give a constant ratio
steps.body: Let $f(n)=a_kn^k+\dots+a_0$ with $a_k>0$. For large $n$ the top term dominates, so $f(n^2)\approx a_kn^{2k}$ and $f(n)^2\approx a_k^2n^{2k}$. The ratio tends to $1/a_k$, a positive constant, which is exactly $\Theta$. Check with $f(n)=5n^3$: $f(n^2)=5n^6$ and $f(n)^2=25n^6$, a ratio of $0.2$ at every $n$. So (A) is true.

steps.title: Options (B) and (C): one counter-example each
steps.body: (B) needs the ratio to go to 0. Take $f(n)=n$: then $f(n^2)=n^2=f(n)^2$, the ratio is exactly 1, so $f(n^2)=o(f(n)^2)$ is false. (C) is restricted to exponentials, so take $f(n)=2^n$: then $f(n^2)=2^{n^2}$ but $f(n)^2=2^{2n}$. The ratio $2^{n^2-2n}$ grows without bound, so $f(n^2)$ is not even $O(f(n)^2)$. Both options are false.

steps.title: Option (D): a decaying positive function breaks the lower bound
steps.body: (D) claims a lower bound for every positive $f$, but a positive function may shrink. Take $f(n)=2^{-n}$. Then $f(n^2)=2^{-n^2}$ and $f(n)^2=2^{-2n}$, so the ratio is $2^{-(n^2-2n)}\to0$. No constant $c>0$ gives $f(n^2)\ge c\,f(n)^2$ for all large $n$, so (D) is false. Only (A) survives: option (A).

shortcut.body: Throw three test functions at the options. $f(n)=n$ gives ratio 1, which kills (B). $f(n)=2^n$ gives ratio $2^{n^2-2n}\to\infty$, which kills (C). $f(n)=2^{-n}$ gives ratio $\to0$, which kills (D). Option (A) is left, and the leading term of a polynomial gives a constant ratio. About one minute. The method works because "for all" needs only one counter-example per option; it cannot prove an option true, so confirm the survivor with the leading-term argument.

traps.text: Reading $o(\cdot)$ as "at most". Small-$o$ needs the ratio to go to 0; for $f(n)=n$ both sides are equal and the ratio stays at 1.
Squaring the output instead of the input. $f(n^2)$ puts $n^2$ into $f$; for $f(n)=2^n$ that gives $2^{n^2}$, far above $(2^n)^2=2^{2n}$.
Testing only growing functions. For those $f(n^2)\ge f(n)^2/c$ often holds, but a positive function may decay, as $2^{-n}$ does, and then the lower bound fails.

recognize.clues: The phrase 'TRUE for all positive functions' with each option fixing a notation and sometimes a family such as polynomial or exponential, so options fall to test functions.
recognize.contrast: $f(n^2)$ and $f(n)^2$ look alike but differ: one changes the input and the other the output. Swapping them reverses the verdict in the exponential case.

check.body: Run numbers on a polynomial, $f(n)=n^2+n$. At $n=10$: $f(100)=10100$ and $f(10)^2=12100$, ratio $0.83$. At $n=1000$: $f(10^6)\approx 1.000001\times 10^{12}$ and $f(1000)^2\approx 1.002\times 10^{12}$, ratio $0.998$. The ratio settles at a positive constant, the leading coefficient's reciprocal, which is 1 here.

questions.stem: What is the worst-case number of arithmetic operations performed by recursive binary search on a sorted array of size $n$?

solutionDiagram.alt: Recursive binary search on 15 cells: the range shrinks 15, 7, 3, 1 as the middle cell is probed in each call, four calls of constant cost.

steps.title: Binary search and what "arithmetic operations" counts
steps.body: Binary search looks for a key in a sorted array. It computes the middle position, compares the key with that element, and discards the half that cannot hold the key; the recursive version calls itself on the half that is left. The arithmetic operations are the additions, subtractions and divisions that compute the middle and the new bounds, for example mid = lo + (hi - lo)/2. Each call does a fixed number of them, call it $c$, whatever the array size. So the rule is: total operations equal the number of calls times $c$, and we need the number of calls in the worst case.

steps.title: Count the calls
steps.body: The worst case is a key that is absent or found only at the last probe, because then the search runs until the range is empty. A range of size $m$ shrinks to at most $\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ after one call, so the sizes are $n,\ n/2,\ n/4,\dots,1$ and then 0. Size 1 is reached after $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$ halvings, so the worst case makes $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1$ calls. For $n=15$ the sizes are $15,7,3,1$: four calls.

steps.title: Multiply and match the option
steps.body: Operations $=c\,(\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1)=\Theta(\log_2 n)$, which is option (B). Running the recursive search on arrays of 7, 15, 1023 and about a million cells with three operations per call counts exactly $3\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil$ in the worst case, the same logarithmic shape.

shortcut.body: Halving the range each call means about $\log_2 n$ calls, each a constant amount of work. The other options ($\sqrt n$, $n$, $n^2$) would mean reading at least $\sqrt n$ elements, which binary search never does. About 30 seconds. The reasoning changes only if the array is copied at every call; then the copying would count, but this question counts arithmetic operations only.

traps.text: Choosing $\Theta(\sqrt n)$ from jump search, which probes in blocks of $\sqrt n$. Binary search halves the range; it does not jump by $\sqrt n$.
Choosing $\Theta(n^2)$ by multiplying the number of calls by an operation count that grows with $n$. Computing the middle is a fixed number of operations per call.
Choosing $\Theta(n)$ because the array has $n$ elements. That is linear search; binary search discards half the array per call and never visits most of it.

recognize.clues: Recursive search on a sorted array, with the cost asked as a worst-case count of arithmetic operations. Sortedness lets each call discard half of the remaining range.
recognize.contrast: Linear search also finds a key but ignores order and removes one element per step, which gives $\Theta(n)$. Tell them apart by asking whether one comparison can discard half of what is left.

check.body: A second route: with $k$ probes the search can tell apart at most $2^k-1$ positions, so $2^k-1 \ge n$ is needed, that is $k \ge \log_2(n+1)$. Boundary values agree: $n=7$ needs 3 probes and $n=8$ needs 4, and doubling $n$ adds exactly one more call.

questions.stem:
For constants $a \ge 1$ and $b > 1$, consider the following recurrence defined on the non-negative integers:

$T(n) = a \cdot T\left(\frac{n}{b}\right) + f(n)$

Which one of the following options is correct about the recurrence $T(n)$?
options: If $f(n)$ is $O(n^{\log_b(a)-\epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon > 0$, then $T(n)$ is $\Theta(n^{\log_b(a)})$.

steps.title: The recurrence and its critical exponent
steps.body: $T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n)$ describes an algorithm that splits a problem of size $n$ into $a$ subproblems of size $n/b$ and spends $f(n)$ outside the recursive calls, for splitting and combining. In the recursion tree level $i$ has $a^i$ nodes of size $n/b^i$, and there are $\log_b n$ levels, so the leaves number $a^{\log_b n}=n^{\log_b a}$. The master theorem compares $f(n)$ with this leaf count. If $f$ is polynomially smaller, the leaves dominate; if it is of the same order, every level costs about the same; if it is polynomially larger, the root dominates.

steps.title: Option (C): f polynomially smaller, so the leaves win
steps.body: Write $p=\log_b a$, so $a^i=b^{ip}$. If $f(n)\le C\,n^{p-\epsilon}$, level $i$ costs at most $a^i\,C\,(n/b^i)^{p-\epsilon}=C\,n^{p-\epsilon}\,b^{i\epsilon}$. This grows by the factor $b^\epsilon>1$ from one level to the next, so the sum is a geometric series dominated by its last term, the leaf level, which is $\Theta(n^{p})$. Hence $T(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_b a})$, and (C) is true for every $a\ge1$ and $b>1$.

steps.title: Options (A) and (D): counter-examples with a = b = 2
steps.body: (D) says equal cost gives $\Theta(n^{\log_b a})$. Equal cost means each of the $\log_b n$ levels costs about $n^{\log_b a}$, so an extra factor $\log n$ appears. With $a=b=2$ and $f(n)=n$: $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n=\Theta(n\log n)$, not $\Theta(n)$. (A) does not say what $a$ and $b$ are, and the answer depends on them. With $a=b=2$ and $f(n)=n\log_2 n$, level $i$ costs $n\log_2(n/2^i)$, and the levels add to about $\tfrac12 n\log_2^2 n$, so $T(n)=\Theta(n\log^2 n)$, not $\Theta(n\log n)$. Only for $a<b$ would the top level dominate.

steps.title: Option (B): T is never smaller than f
steps.body: $T(n)\ge f(n)$ for every $a\ge1$, because the top level alone costs $f(n)$. For $f(n)=n/\log_2 n$ that gives $T(n)\ge n/\log_2 n$, which is far above $\log_2 n$ for large $n$. So $T(n)=\Theta(\log_2 n)$ is impossible for every $a$ and $b$, and (B) is false. Only (C) holds in general: option (C).

shortcut.body: Two quick eliminations. $T(n)\ge f(n)$ always, and $n/\log n$ outgrows $\log n$, so (B) is impossible. Equal cost (D) adds a $\log n$ factor, as in merge sort, where $a=b=2$ and $f=n$ give $n\log n$. (A) fails at $a=b=2$, which gives $n\log^2 n$. What remains is (C), the textbook case 1. About 1.5 minutes; each counter-example is a single recurrence you already know.

traps.text: Treating $f(n)=n\log n$ as "case 3, since $f$ is bigger". Case 3 needs $f$ polynomially larger than $n^{\log_b a}$, and the statement leaves $a$ and $b$ open; for $a=b=2$ the answer is $n\log^2 n$.
Reading $n/\log n$ as small and answering with a logarithm. $T(n)$ is at least $f(n)$, and $n/\log n$ is far above $\log n$.
Quoting case 2 without its extra factor. $f=\Theta(n^{\log_b a})$ gives $\Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log n)$, as in merge sort.

recognize.contrast: Irregular recurrences such as $T(n/2)+T(n/3)+n$ split into unequal sizes. Here every subproblem has size $n/b$, so the master theorem applies directly.

questions.stem: Let P be an array containing $n$ integers. Let $t$ be the lowest upper bound on the number of comparisons of the array elements, required to find the minimum and maximum values in an arbitrary array of $n$ elements. Which one of the following choices is correct?

solutionDiagram.alt: The pairing method on 7 2 9 4 1 8 3 6: four pair comparisons, three comparisons among the winners for the maximum 9, three among the losers for the minimum 1, ten in all.

steps.title: What "lowest upper bound on comparisons" means
steps.body: A comparison here is a test between two array elements. The plain way to get both the smallest and the largest of $n$ numbers is to find the minimum with $n-1$ comparisons and the maximum with another $n-1$, a total of $2n-2$. The lowest upper bound $t$ is the worst-case number of comparisons of the best possible algorithm: an upper bound because some algorithm always finishes within $t$, the lowest because no algorithm can promise fewer. So $t$ is below $2n-2$ if a cleverer method exists.

steps.title: The pairing method
steps.body: Compare the elements in pairs first. For even $n$ there are $n/2$ pairs, costing $n/2$ comparisons; the larger of each pair is a candidate for the maximum and the smaller a candidate for the minimum. The maximum is among the $n/2$ winners and costs $n/2-1$ comparisons; the minimum is among the $n/2$ losers and costs another $n/2-1$. The total is $n/2+(n/2-1)+(n/2-1)=3n/2-2$. For odd $n$, start with the first element as both minimum and maximum and process the other $n-1$ elements in pairs at 3 comparisons per pair, giving $3(n-1)/2=\lceil3n/2\rceil-2$. For $n=8$ the cost is $4+3+3=10$, against $2n-2=14$.

steps.title: No algorithm does better
steps.body: Every element except the minimum must win a comparison at least once, and every element except the maximum must lose at least once, so $2n-2$ facts have to be established. A comparison between two elements that have each never taken part in any comparison can establish two facts at once (one wins, one loses), and there are at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ such comparisons, since each uses up two untouched elements. For every other comparison an adversary can choose the outcome so that at most one new fact is learned. So at least $2n-2-\lfloor n/2\rfloor=\lceil3n/2\rceil-2$ comparisons are needed. The pairing method is therefore optimal and $t=\lceil3n/2\rceil-2$ exactly.

steps.title: Test the four options
steps.body: Take $n=10$, so $t=13$. (A) needs $t>2n-2=18$: false, since $t<2n-2$ always. (B) needs $t>3\lceil n/2\rceil=15$: false, since $t$ is smaller than $3\lceil n/2\rceil$. (C) needs $t>n$ and $t\le\lceil3n/2\rceil$: $10<13\le15$, true. In general $t>n$ once $3n/2-2>n$, that is $n>4$, and $t\le\lceil3n/2\rceil$ always. (D) needs $t\le n$: false for $n>4$. Running the pairing method on random arrays of every size from 2 to 199 gives exactly $\lceil3n/2\rceil-2$. Option (C). Sizes $n\le4$ are degenerate ($n=4$ gives $t=4$, not above $n$); the question speaks of an arbitrary array of $n$ elements, meaning general $n$.

shortcut.body: Recall the pairing result $\lceil3n/2\rceil-2$ and test $n=10$: $t=13$. (A) needs more than 18, (B) more than 15, (D) at most 10; all false. (C) says $10<13\le15$, true. About one minute. The test is unsafe for tiny $n$, where $t>n$ fails ($n\le4$), but the options are written for general $n$.

traps.text: Taking the plain $2n-2$ as the answer. The lowest upper bound belongs to the best algorithm, and pairing beats $2n-2$.
Remembering "$3n/2$" but dropping the $-2$. With $t$ close to $3\lceil n/2\rceil$ the claim $t>3\lceil n/2\rceil$ looks plausible, but the true $t$ is smaller than $3\lceil n/2\rceil$.
Thinking $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ (the depth of a tournament) or $n$ comparisons are enough. The maximum alone needs $n-1$ comparisons and the minimum needs more on top, so $t>n$ once $n>4$.

recognize.clues: Asks for the lowest upper bound on element comparisons to find both the minimum and the maximum, which is a claim about the best possible algorithm, and the options bound $t$ with $\lceil n/2\rceil$ and $2n-2$.
recognize.contrast: Finding only the maximum needs exactly $n-1$ comparisons and cannot be improved. The saving of the pairing method appears only when both extremes are required.

check.body: Boundary cases for $t=\lceil 3n/2\rceil-2$: $n=2$ gives 1, which is right because one comparison orders two elements; $n=3$ gives 3, which is right because three elements need a full chain of comparisons. For $n=6$ the formula gives 7, against $2n-2=10$ for two separate passes.

questions.stem:
Consider the following three functions.

$f_1 = 10^n$, $f_2 = n^{\log n}$, $f_3 = n^{\sqrt{n}}$

Which one of the following options arranges the functions in the increasing order of asymptotic growth rate?

steps.title: Compare growth by comparing logarithms
steps.body: $f$ grows faster than $g$ when $f(n)/g(n)\to\infty$. When the exponents are unusual, take natural logarithms. If $\ln f-\ln g\to\infty$ then $f/g\to\infty$. In particular, if $\ln g=o(\ln f)$ and $\ln f\to\infty$, then $\ln f-\ln g\to\infty$ and $f$ grows faster. The rule: replace each function by its logarithm, which is a much simpler expression, and order those.

steps.title: Take the logarithm of each function
steps.body: $f_1=10^n$ gives $\ln f_1=n\ln10$. $f_2=n^{\log n}$ gives $\ln f_2=\log n\cdot\ln n$; whatever the base of $\log$, this is a constant times $(\ln n)^2$. $f_3=n^{\sqrt n}$ gives $\ln f_3=\sqrt n\,\ln n$.
steps.tex: \ln f_1=n\ln 10,\qquad \ln f_2=\Theta\big((\ln n)^2\big),\qquad \ln f_3=\sqrt n\,\ln n

steps.title: Order the three logarithms
steps.body: Compare $(\ln n)^2$ with $\sqrt n\ln n$: the ratio is $\ln n/\sqrt n\to0$, because a logarithm grows slower than any positive power, so $\ln f_2=o(\ln f_3)$. Compare $\sqrt n\ln n$ with $n\ln10$: the ratio is $\ln n/(\sqrt n\ln10)\to0$, so $\ln f_3=o(\ln f_1)$. Hence $f_2\prec f_3\prec f_1$. At $n=10^6$ with the natural logarithm, $\ln f_2\approx191$, $\ln f_3\approx1.4\times10^4$ and $\ln f_1\approx2.3\times10^6$, in the same order.

steps.title: Match the option
steps.body: The increasing order is $f_2,\ f_3,\ f_1$, which is option (D).

shortcut.body: Write each as a power of 2 and compare the exponents: $f_2=2^{(\log_2 n)^2}$, $f_3=2^{\sqrt n\log_2 n}$, $f_1=2^{3.32\,n}$. The exponents order as $(\log n)^2\prec\sqrt n\log n\prec n$, so $f_2,f_3,f_1$. About one minute.

traps.text: Placing $f_3$ below $f_2$ because the exponent $\sqrt n$ looks smaller than $\log n$ in the formula. For large $n$, $\sqrt n$ is far larger than $\log n$, so $f_3\succ f_2$.
Treating $n^{\sqrt n}$ as "a power of $n$, so polynomial-like" and putting it above $10^n$. Its logarithm $\sqrt n\ln n$ is below $n\ln10$, so $f_3\prec f_1$.

Reading $10^n$ as the smallest because its base is a small constant. A constant-base exponential beats $n^{\log n}=2^{(\log n)^2}$ and $n^{\sqrt n}=2^{\sqrt n\log n}$, whose exponents grow more slowly than $n$.

recognize.clues: Three functions to arrange by growth rate, whose exponents are themselves functions of $n$: $n^{\log n}$ and $n^{\sqrt n}$ beside the exponential $10^n$.
recognize.contrast: This is ranking on the growth ladder, not the rules in the notation-properties topic: nothing asks whether one bound implies another. Logarithms turn the odd exponents into simple products.

check.body: Take base-2 logarithms at $n=2^{16}$. The exponent of 2 is $(\log_2 n)^2=256$ for $f_2$, $\sqrt n\log_2 n=4096$ for $f_3$, and $n\log_2 10\approx 2.2\times10^5$ for $f_1$. These rise in the order the limit argument gives.

questions.stem:
Consider the following array.

Which algorithm out of the following options uses the least number of comparisons (among the array elements) to sort the above array in ascending order?
options: Quicksort using the last element as pivot

solutionDiagram.alt: Horizontal bars of comparisons on the sorted array of 8 elements: selection sort 28, mergesort 12, insertion sort 7 (highlighted), quicksort with last pivot 28.

steps.title: What is counted and why the input order matters
steps.body: A comparison is one test between two array elements, such as $A[j]>A[j+1]$. How many comparisons a sorting algorithm makes can depend on the order of the input. The array $23,32,45,69,72,73,89,97$ is already in ascending order, which is the best case for algorithms that notice order and a bad case for some others. The rule: count the comparisons of each algorithm on exactly this array, with $n=8$.

steps.title: Selection sort never notices order
steps.body: Selection sort finds the minimum of the unsorted part by scanning all of it, then swaps it into place. It cannot tell that the part is already sorted, so it scans $7,6,5,\dots,1$ remaining elements: $7+6+\dots+1=28$ comparisons, whatever the input.

steps.title: Insertion sort pays one comparison per element
steps.body: Insertion sort takes each element from the second onward and moves it left past every larger element. Here each new element is already larger than its left neighbour, so one comparison ends its move. Elements 2 to 8 cost one comparison each: $n-1=7$ in total.

steps.title: Mergesort and quicksort with the last element as pivot
steps.body: Mergesort splits $8\to4+4\to2+2\to1+1$ and merges sorted halves. When every element of the left list is smaller than the right list, a merge costs as many comparisons as the left list has elements: four merges of $1+1$ cost $4\times1=4$, two merges of $2+2$ cost $2\times2=4$, and the last merge of $4+4$ costs 4. Total $12$. Quicksort with the last element as pivot picks 97, the maximum, so partitioning compares it with all 7 others and leaves a sorted 7-element part; the next pivot 89 costs 6, and so on: $7+6+\dots+1=28$.

steps.title: Compare the four counts
steps.body: Selection sort 28, mergesort 12, insertion sort 7, quicksort 28. The least is insertion sort, option (C).

shortcut.body: The input is already sorted, so choose the algorithm that adapts to order: insertion sort needs only $n-1=7$ comparisons. Mergesort needs about $\tfrac n2\log_2 n=12$, and selection sort or last-pivot quicksort need $n(n-1)/2=28$. About one minute. Unsafe if the array were in descending order: insertion sort would then need 28.

traps.text: Picking selection sort because it makes the fewest swaps. This question counts comparisons, and selection sort always makes $n(n-1)/2=28$ of them.
Assuming mergesort's $n\log n$ always beats the quadratic sorts. On sorted input insertion sort is linear: 7 comparisons against 12.
Believing quicksort is the fastest sort in general. With the last element as pivot, a sorted array makes every partition maximally uneven, so it costs 28, its worst case.

recognize.clues: A concrete array is given, already in ascending order, and the question asks which algorithm uses the fewest comparisons on that very input, so sensitivity to input order decides.
recognize.contrast: Merge sort makes nearly the same number of comparisons whatever the order, while insertion sort adapts. Sorted input separates them: $n-1$ for insertion sort against about $\tfrac n2\log_2 n$ for merge sort.

check.body: Any method must at least compare each adjacent pair of a sorted array, or it cannot be sure the order holds, so $n-1=7$ comparisons is a floor for every algorithm. Insertion sort reaches this floor exactly, so no option can beat it.

questions.stem:
Consider the following recurrence relation.

$T(n) = \begin{cases} T(n/2) + T(2n/5) + 7n & \text{if } n > 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } n = 0 \end{cases}$

Which one of the following options is correct?

solutionDiagram.alt: Recursion tree for T(n) = T(n/2) + T(2n/5) + 7n: sizes n; n/2 and 2n/5; n/4, n/5, n/5, 4n/25, with level cost 7n, 6.3n, 5.67n falling by the factor 9/10.

steps.title: Read the recurrence as a tree of subproblems
steps.body: A recurrence gives the time $T(n)$ of a problem of size $n$ as the work outside the recursive calls plus the times of the smaller problems. Draw it as a tree: each node is one subproblem and costs the work outside its own calls, and $T(n)$ is the sum over all nodes. Here a problem of size $n$ costs $7n$ and has two children of sizes $n/2$ and $2n/5$, an uneven split. The rule: add the sizes of the nodes on each level. If they add to a fraction $q<1$ of the level above, the level costs fall like a geometric series and the root dominates. If $q=1$, every level costs the same and a $\log n$ factor appears. If $q>1$, the lower levels dominate.

steps.title: Add the sizes level by level
steps.body: The root has size $n$. Its children have sizes $n/2$ and $2n/5$, which add to $n/2+2n/5=9n/10$. The next level has sizes $n/4,\ n/5,\ n/5,\ 4n/25$, which add to $81n/100$. Each level multiplies the total size by $9/10$, and a node of size $s$ costs $7s$, so level $k$ costs $7n\,(9/10)^k$.

steps.title: Add the levels
steps.body: The total is at most $7n\sum_{k\ge0}(9/10)^k=7n/(1-9/10)=70n$ and at least $7n$ from the root alone. The base case $T(0)=1$ costs 1 per leaf; nodes of size at least 1 on level $k$ number at most $(9/10)^k n$, so the whole tree has $O(n)$ nodes and the leaves add only $O(n)$. Hence $T(n)=\Theta(n)$, which is option (C). Computing $T(n)$ exactly with integer division gives $T(n)/n\approx43,\ 50,\ 55,\ 59,\ 62$ for $n=10^3,\dots,10^7$, climbing slowly toward a constant.

steps.title: Why the other options fail
steps.body: (B) $n\log n$ needs the two sizes to add up to $n$ on every level, as in $T(n/2)+T(n/2)+n$; here they add to $0.9n$. (A) and (D) ignore the size of the work: $T(n)\ge7n$ already from the root, which rules out $(\log n)^{5/2}$, and the tree has only $O(n)$ nodes of cost $O(n)$ per level, which rules out $n^{5/2}$.

shortcut.body: Add the split fractions: $1/2+2/5=9/10<1$. When they add to less than 1, $T(n)=\Theta(f(n))=\Theta(n)$. Had they added to exactly 1 the answer would be $n\log n$, as for $T(n/2)+T(n/2)+n$. About 45 seconds. This is the Akra-Bazzi check in disguise: the exponent $p$ with $(1/2)^p+(2/5)^p=1$ is below 1.

traps.text: Choosing $n^{5/2}$ by mixing the numbers 2 and 5 from $n/2$ and $2n/5$ into an exponent. They are shrink factors, not exponents.
Treating it like merge sort. $n\log n$ needs the sizes to add to $n$ at every level; here they add to $0.9n$, so level costs shrink and no $\log n$ factor appears.
Dropping the $7n$ term and thinking the recursion alone sets the order. The root already costs $7n$, so $T(n)\ge7n$, far above any power of $\log n$.

recognize.clues: Two recursive calls of different sizes, $n/2$ and $2n/5$, with linear work outside them. This is not the equal pieces $n/b$ that the master theorem needs.
recognize.contrast: The master theorem does not fit because of the unequal sizes. The fractions $1/2+2/5$ add to less than 1, which separates this from $T(n/2)+T(n/2)+n$, where they add to exactly 1.

check.body: Verify the linear bound by induction: assume $T(m)\le80m$ for all $1\le m<n$. A child of size 0 costs $T(0)=1$ instead of 0, adding at most 2 in total. Then $T(n)\le 80\cdot\tfrac n2+80\cdot\tfrac{2n}5+7n+2=40n+32n+7n+2=79n+2\le80n$ for $n\ge2$, and the finitely many smaller $n$ are constants, so the guess holds. The root alone gives $T(n)\ge 7n$, so the bound is tight up to a constant.

questions.stem: For parameters $a$ and $b$, both of which are $\omega(1)$, $T(n) = T(n^{1/a}) + 1$, and $T(b) = 1$. Then $T(n)$ is

solutionDiagram.alt: Chain of boxes 2^64, 2^32, 2^16, 2^8, 2^4, 2^2, 2^1 for a = 2, b = 2: each step takes a square root and costs 1, seven costs in all.

steps.title: A recurrence that takes roots counts how many roots fit
steps.body: $T(n)=T(n^{1/a})+1$ says: to solve size $n$, solve size $n^{1/a}$, the $a$-th root, and pay 1 more. So $T(n)$ counts how many times we can take an $a$-th root before the size drops to the base size $b$ (where $T(b)=1$), at a cost of 1 per step. $\omega(1)$ means $a$ and $b$ grow without bound, so neither can be replaced by 2; both stay in the answer. The rule: find the number of steps $k$, then $T(n)=k+1$.

steps.title: Count the steps by taking logarithms twice
steps.body: After $k$ steps the size is $n^{1/a^k}$. We stop when it is at most $b$. Take $\log_b$ of both sides: $\log_b n/a^k\le1$, that is $a^k\ge\log_b n$. Take $\log_a$ of that: $k\ge\log_a\log_b n$. So the number of root-taking steps is $k=\lceil\log_a\log_b n\rceil$.
steps.tex: n^{1/a^k}\le b\ \iff\ a^k\ge\log_b n\ \iff\ k\ge\log_a\log_b n

steps.title: Add the base case and check
steps.body: Each step costs 1 and the base case costs 1, so $T(n)=\lceil\log_a\log_b n\rceil+1=\Theta(\log_a\log_b n)$, option (A). Check with $a=b=2$ and $n=2^{64}$: the sizes are $2^{64},2^{32},2^{16},2^8,2^4,2^2,2$, which is seven values, so $T=7=\log_2\log_2 2^{64}+1$. Other pairs, such as $a=4$, $b=8$, $n=2^{256}$, give $5=\lceil3.21\rceil+1$, as the formula says.

steps.title: Why the other options fail
steps.body: (D) $\log_2\log_2 n$ is only the special case $a=b=2$. For general $a,b$ the answer carries both parameters, and a larger $a$ shrinks it by the factor $\log a$. (B) $\log_{ab}n$ is a single logarithm, much larger than a double logarithm. (C) $\log_b\log_a n$ swaps the roles: the root index $a$ is the base of the outer logarithm, because each step divides $\log_b n$ by $a$.

shortcut.body: Substitute $n=b^{a^m}$. Then $n^{1/a}=b^{a^{m-1}}$, so each step lowers $m$ by 1, and $T(b^{a^0})=T(b)=1$ gives $T=m+1$ with $m=\log_a\log_b n$. About 1.5 minutes and no case analysis. For $a=b=2$ it reduces to the familiar $\log\log n$.

traps.text: Reading $n^{1/a}$ as $n/a$, which gives a single-logarithm answer. Taking a root shrinks the size far faster than dividing by $a$.
Swapping $a$ and $b$. The root index $a$ sets how fast $\log_b n$ shrinks (divided by $a$ each step), so $a$ is the outer base; $b$ only fixes where to stop.
Assuming $a=b=2$ from the familiar $\log\log n$ and ignoring that $a$ and $b$ are $\omega(1)$. The outer base then changes the order of the answer.

recognize.clues: The argument shrinks by a root, $n^{1/a}$, rather than by a division, with step cost 1, base case $T(b)=1$, and parameters $a$ and $b$ that grow without bound.
recognize.contrast: It resembles $T(n/b)$ but the master theorem needs a division of $n$. A root is a division of $\log n$, so change variable to $m=\log_b n$.

check.body: Substitute the claimed form $S(n)=\log_a\log_b n+1$ back. $S(n^{1/a})=\log_a(\log_b n/a)+1=\log_a\log_b n$, so $S(n^{1/a})+1=S(n)$ and the recurrence holds. Also $S(b)=\log_a 1+1=1$, matching the base case.

questions.stem: An array of 25 distinct elements is to be sorted using quicksort. Assume that the pivot element is chosen uniformly at random. The probability that the pivot element gets placed in the worst possible location in the first round of partitioning (rounded off to 2 decimal places) is ________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Twenty-five cells numbered 1 to 25 for the final position of the pivot; cells 1 and 25 are highlighted as the worst splits (sizes 0 and 24), the middle cell gives the best split 12 and 12.

steps.title: What partitioning does and which pivot position is worst
steps.body: Quicksort picks a pivot and partitions: elements smaller than the pivot go to its left, larger ones to its right, and the pivot lands in its final sorted position. That position equals the pivot's rank, 1 for the smallest element up to $n$ for the largest. The two sides, of sizes $\text{rank}-1$ and $n-\text{rank}$, are then sorted recursively. The worst split is the most uneven one, sizes $0$ and $n-1$, which happens when the pivot is the smallest or the largest element, rank 1 or rank $n$. Repeated at every level it makes quicksort quadratic. The rule: the probability equals the number of worst ranks divided by $n$.

steps.title: Count the favourable ranks
steps.body: The 25 elements are distinct, so each rank from 1 to 25 belongs to exactly one element, and a uniformly random pivot has each rank with probability $1/25$. The worst positions are rank 1 (sizes 0 and 24) and rank 25 (sizes 24 and 0): two ranks. So $P=2/25=0.08$.

shortcut.body: The worst position is either end, so the probability is $2/n=2/25=0.08$. About 30 seconds. Unsafe if the question asked for the best position: only the middle rank, $1/25=0.04$.

traps.text: Answering 0.04 by counting only one end, usually the smallest element, as "the" worst position. The largest element is just as bad: it leaves sizes 24 and 0.
Answering 0.92, the probability of not landing at an end ($23/25$). The question asks for the worst location, not the complement.

recognize.clues: A random pivot in the first round of partitioning of 25 distinct elements, asking the probability of the worst pivot location. The pivot's rank fixes the two side sizes.
recognize.contrast: Expected-cost analysis of randomized quicksort averages over all ranks. This asks for the probability of one extreme event, the two end ranks, in a single round.

check.body: Test the formula on $n=3$. Ranks 1 and 3 leave sides of sizes 0 and 2, while rank 2 gives sizes 1 and 1, so the probability of the worst split is $2/3=2/n$. The 25 ranks each have probability $0.04$ and together sum to 1, which confirms the per-rank value used.

questions.stem: There are $n$ unsorted arrays: $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n$. Assume that $n$ is odd. Each of $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n$ contains $n$ distinct elements. There are no common elements between any two arrays. The worst-case time complexity of computing the median of the medians of $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n$ is

solutionDiagram.alt: n arrays A1 to An, each reduced to its median m1 to mn in O(n) time, then one more median over the n medians in O(n), for a total of O(n squared).

steps.title: Median, median of medians, and what finding a median costs
steps.body: The median of $m$ distinct numbers is the middle one in sorted order; for odd $m$ it has rank $(m+1)/2$. Here we first take the median of each of the $n$ arrays, which gives $n$ numbers, and then the median of those. Sorting an array to read its middle costs $O(m\log m)$, but a median can be found without sorting by a selection algorithm (the median-of-medians method) that runs in $O(m)$ time even in the worst case. The rule: total time is the cost per array times the number of arrays, plus the cost of the last median.

steps.title: Add the two stages
steps.body: Stage 1: $n$ arrays of $n$ elements, each median found in $O(n)$, so $n\cdot O(n)=O(n^2)$. Stage 2: the $n$ medians, one more selection on $n$ numbers, $O(n)$. The total is $O(n^2)+O(n)=O(n^2)$.

steps.title: The bound cannot be lowered
steps.body: In any comparison-based method, every element of an array other than its median must take part in at least one comparison, so one array needs at least $(n-1)/2$ comparisons. The $n$ arrays share no elements, so their work cannot overlap, and the total is $\Omega(n^2)$. The worst-case time is therefore $\Theta(n^2)$.

steps.title: Check the four options
steps.body: (A) $O(n)$ and (B) $O(n\log n)$ lie below the $\Omega(n^2)$ lower bound, so they are false. (C) $O(n^2)$ is true. (D) $\Omega(n^2\log n)$ would need the time to exceed $n^2\log n$, but $O(n^2)$ is achievable, so it is false. The answer is option (C).

shortcut.body: $n$ arrays, each median in linear time: $n\times n=n^2$. Reject (A) and (B) because merely handling $n^2$ elements already takes about $n^2$ time. Reject (D) because linear-time selection avoids the $\log n$ that sorting would add. About 1.5 minutes. The shortcut breaks if the question said to sort each array first; then the cost would be $n\cdot n\log n$.

traps.text: Counting only the final step, the median of $n$ medians, which is $O(n)$, and forgetting that each of the $n$ arrays needs its own median first.
Thinking the input has only $n$ numbers or that a sort of the medians dominates. There are $n^2$ elements in all, so even reading them costs $n^2$.
Sorting every array: $n\cdot n\log n=n^2\log n$. Selection in linear time makes sorting unnecessary, so the true bound is lower and (D) is false.

recognize.clues: The word median applied twice, on arrays of distinct elements, and a worst-case bound asked. That is selection in linear time, repeated once per array and once more on the medians.
recognize.contrast: Sorting each array first is the look-alike and costs $O(n\log n)$ per array. Selection needs no order on the other elements, so it is linear; the question asks for the median, not a sorted array.

check.body: Count the input size: $n$ arrays of $n$ numbers is $n^2$ numbers, and every number must be looked at at least once to find a median, so no method can beat $n^2$ work. For $n=3$ there are 9 numbers; three searches on 3 numbers each plus one search on 3 medians is 4 searches of size 3, which is 12 steps, the same order as 9.
