questions.stem: Match the algorithms with their time complexities:

rows: (R) Heap sort given $n$ numbers at the worst case

steps.title: What a time complexity says and the ladder of rungs
steps.body: The time complexity of an algorithm is how its number of basic steps grows with the input size $n$. For Hanoi $n$ is the number of disks, for the matrix problem it is the side of the matrix. Growth rates sit on a ladder from slow to fast: $\log n$, $n$, $n\log n$, $n^2$, $2^n$. The rule for each item: find the basic operation, count how often it runs as a function of $n$, and read off the rung.

steps.title: P and Q, the two recursive algorithms
steps.body: Towers of Hanoi with $n$ disks moves $n-1$ disks, then one disk, then $n-1$ disks again: $M(n)=2M(n-1)+1$, which solves to $2^n-1=\Theta(2^n)$, item (iii). Binary search halves the range at every probe, so it needs at most $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor+1$ probes, $\Theta(\log n)$, item (iv). The difference is the recursion shape: Hanoi makes two calls on size $n-1$, binary search makes one call on half the size.

steps.title: R and S
steps.body: Heap sort builds a heap in $O(n)$ and then does $n$ extract-max steps of $O(\log n)$ each, so even in the worst case it takes $\Theta(n\log n)$, item (ii). Counting the comparisons of a heap sort on random arrays of 1000, 4000 and 16000 numbers gives $1.69,\ 1.74,\ 1.78$ times $n\log_2 n$, with no sign of $n^2$. Adding two $n\times n$ matrices adds $n^2$ pairs of entries, one addition each, so $\Theta(n^2)$, item (i).

steps.title: Assemble the matching
steps.body: P is (iii), Q is (iv), R is (ii), S is (i). That is option (C).

shortcut.body: Pin down the extremes first: Hanoi is the only exponential, (iii), and binary search the only logarithm, (iv). That leaves options (A) and (C), which differ on R and S. Matrix addition touches $n^2$ entries, so S is (i), which gives (C). About one minute.

traps.text: Giving heap sort $n^2$ (confusing it with bubble or insertion sort) and matrix addition $n\log n$. Heap sort is $n\log n$ even in the worst case, and matrix addition is one operation per entry on $n^2$ entries.

Swapping Hanoi and binary search, and also swapping heap sort with matrix addition. Binary search has one recursive call on half the input, which is logarithmic; Hanoi has two calls on size $n-1$, which is exponential. Heap sort is $n\log n$ (item ii) and matrix addition is $n^2$ (item i), the reverse of what this option says.
Swapping only Hanoi and binary search. R and S are placed correctly, but P and Q are not: Hanoi is exponential and binary search is logarithmic.

recognize.clues: A matching of four named algorithms to Theta classes, with one logarithmic, one exponential, one $n\log n$ and one quadratic. The task is ordering growth rates, not solving a recurrence in detail.
recognize.contrast: Heap sort and matrix addition are both polynomial and easy to swap. Heap sort does $n$ extractions of cost $\log n$ each, while matrix addition does one step per entry of an $n\times n$ grid.

check.body: Substitute $n=20$. Hanoi needs $2^{20}-1$, about a million moves; binary search at most 5 probes; heap sort about $20\log_2 20\approx 86$ units of work; matrix addition $400$ additions. The sizes rank as 5, 86, 400, a million, and each matches its stated class, so the pairing is consistent.

questions.stem:
Consider the recurrence function

$T(n) = \begin{cases} 2T(\sqrt{n}) + 1, & n > 2 \\ 2, & 0 < n \le 2 \end{cases}$

Then $T(n)$ in terms of $\Theta$ notation is

solutionDiagram.alt: Recursion tree for T(n) = 2T(sqrt n) + 1 with n = 2^16: levels 2^16, two of 2^8, four of 2^4, eight of 2^2, sixteen leaves 2^1; 15 internal nodes of cost 1 and 16 leaves of cost 2 give 47.

steps.title: A square-root recurrence needs a change of variable
steps.body: $T(n)=2T(\sqrt n)+1$ shrinks the size by taking a square root, not by dividing, so the master theorem does not apply directly. The trick is to rename the size so that the square root becomes a halving. Put $n=2^m$, so $m=\log_2 n$ and $\sqrt n=2^{m/2}$, and define $S(m)=T(2^m)$. The rule: solve the new recurrence in $m$, then replace $m$ by $\log_2 n$.

steps.title: Rewrite the recurrence in m
steps.body: $T(2^m)=2T(2^{m/2})+1$ becomes $S(m)=2S(m/2)+1$. The condition $n>2$ becomes $m>1$, and $T(n)=2$ for $0<n\le2$ becomes $S(m)=2$ for $0<m\le1$.

steps.title: Solve for S and go back to n
steps.body: Now $a=2$, $b=2$ and $f(m)=1$. Since $m^{\log_2 2}=m$ is polynomially larger than $f$, the master theorem gives $S(m)=\Theta(m)$. Exactly, for $m=2^k$: $S(1)=2$, $S(2)=5$, $S(4)=11$, $S(8)=23$, each time $S(2m)=2S(m)+1$, which gives $S(m)=3m-1$. Back in $n$, $T(n)=3\log_2 n-1=\Theta(\log n)$. Computing $T(2^{2^k})$ directly for $k=0,\dots,6$ gives $2,5,11,23,47,95,191$, which equals $3\log_2 n-1$ each time.

steps.title: Why the answer is not log log n
steps.body: The recursion depth is only $\log_2\log_2 n$, because the exponent $m$ is halved at each level. But every call makes two calls, so the number of leaves is $2^{\log_2\log_2 n}=\log_2 n$. Depth alone would suggest $\log\log n$; the doubling turns it into $\log n$. For $n=2^{16}$ the tree has 15 internal nodes and 16 leaves.

shortcut.body: Unroll twice: $T(n)=2T(n^{1/2})+1=4T(n^{1/4})+3=8T(n^{1/8})+7$. The factor in front is $2^k$, and the unrolling stops when $n^{1/2^k}\le2$, that is $2^k\approx\log_2 n$. So $T=\Theta(\log n)$. About 1.5 minutes.

traps.text: Stopping at the depth $\log_2\log_2 n$ and forgetting that each level doubles the number of calls: $2^{\log\log n}=\log n$.
Matching the $\sqrt n$ in the recurrence with the answer. The $\sqrt n$ is the size of the subproblem, not the running time.
Treating it as $2T(n/2)+1$, which is $\Theta(n)$. Here the size shrinks to $\sqrt n$, much faster than $n/2$.

recognize.clues: The subproblem size is $\sqrt n$ and the combine cost is a constant. A change of variable $n=2^m$ is the signal that a master-theorem form hides inside.
recognize.contrast: The look-alike is $T(n)=2T(n/2)+1$, which is linear in $n$. A square root shrinks the size much faster, so the same two calls produce a count in $\log n$ instead.

check.body: Unroll by hand instead of climbing the chain. After $k$ steps $T(n)=2^kT(n^{1/2^k})+2^k-1$. For $n=2^{16}$ and $k=4$ the size is $n^{1/16}=2$, so $T=16\cdot T(2)+15=16\cdot2+15=47$. Here $2^k=16=\log_2 n$, so the count of leaves is $\log_2 n$ and the growth is $\Theta(\log n)$.

questions.stem:
Consider the following C function.

Time complexity of fun in terms of $\Theta$ notation is

solutionDiagram.alt: Bar chart of the inner-loop iteration counts for n = 16 and i from 1 to 16: 15, 8, 5, 4, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, totalling 57, the harmonic shape n over i.

steps.title: Count the innermost statement, summing inner counts over the outer variable
steps.body: To find a loop nest's time, count how many times the innermost statement runs as a function of $n$; here that is the printf. When the inner loop's count depends on the outer variable, add the inner counts over every value of the outer variable. The loop j = 1; j < n; j += i visits $1,\ 1+i,\ 1+2i,\dots$ for as long as the value is below $n$.

steps.title: Inner count for a fixed i
steps.body: The visited values are $1+ti$ for $t=0,1,2,\dots$, and they must satisfy $1+ti<n$, that is $t<(n-1)/i$. So the inner loop runs $\lceil(n-1)/i\rceil$ times, between $(n-1)/i$ and $(n-1)/i+1$. For $n=16$ the counts for $i=1,\dots,16$ are $15,8,5,4,3,3,3,2,2,2,2,2,2,2,1,1$.

steps.title: Sum over i: a harmonic sum
steps.body: The total is $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lceil(n-1)/i\rceil$. It is at least $(n-1)H_n$ and at most $(n-1)H_n+n$, where $H_n=1+\tfrac12+\dots+\tfrac1n=\ln n+O(1)$ is the harmonic number. So the total is $\Theta(n\log n)$. The exact total is 57 for $n=16$; for $n=100,\ 1000,\ 10000$ it is $567,\ 8045,\ 103631$, and dividing by $n\log_2 n$ gives $0.85,\ 0.81,\ 0.78$, a bounded ratio. The answer is option (C).

shortcut.body: The inner loop runs about $n/i$ times, so the total is $n(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac13+\dots)=n\ln n$. Remember the pattern: a step of $i$ over a range of $n$, summed over $i$, is a harmonic sum and gives $n\log n$. About one minute.

traps.text: Choosing $n\sqrt n$ by treating the small values of $i$ as costing a full $n$ each. Small $i$ cost $n/i$, not $n$, and the harmonic sum is only about $\ln n$.
Taking the inner loop as $n$ iterations and ignoring the step $i$, which gives $n\times n=n^2$. The step $i$ cuts the count to $n/i$.
Multiplying $n\log n$ by another factor $n$, or reading the inner loop as $\log n$ per $i$ on top of the harmonic sum. The sum over $i$ already includes the outer loop.

recognize.clues: A nested loop whose inner step is the outer variable, written j += i. The inner count is then $n/i$, which marks a harmonic sum rather than a plain product of two ranges.
recognize.contrast: If the inner step were fixed, the loops would multiply to $n^2$. If the outer variable doubled each time, the sum would be geometric and linear. A step of $i$ for each $i=1,2,3,\dots$ gives the harmonic case.

check.body: Bound the sum by an integral. Since $\ln(n+1)\le H_n\le1+\ln n$, the total lies between $(n-1)\ln(n+1)$ and $(n-1)(1+\ln n)+n$. For $n=16$ that is between 42.5 and 72.6, and the counted total 57 is inside. Both bounds are $\Theta(n\log n)$, while $n^2=256$ and $n\sqrt n=64$ miss the pattern as $n$ grows.

When the inner loop count depends on the outer variable, the total is the sum of the inner counts over all values of the outer variable.
A loop that starts at 1 and steps by $i$ while staying below $n$ runs about $n/i$ times. Adding these counts over $i$ is a harmonic sum.
Write the inner count as a function of $i$, then write the total as a sum from $i=1$ to $n$. Pull the common factor $n$ out of the sum.
The total is about $n\left(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac13+\dots+\tfrac1n\right)$. Decide how the bracket grows with $n$ and multiply back by $n$.

variation.explanation: The outer variable takes the values $1,2,4,\dots$, and for each $i$ the inner loop runs about $n/i$ times. The total is $n(1+\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\dots)$, a geometric series with sum below $2n$, so the time is $\Theta(n)$. Counting by a program gives about $2n$ for $n=10^3, 10^5, 10^7$. Choosing $n\log n$ treats the sum as harmonic, $n^2$ ignores the step $i$, and $\log n$ counts only the outer loop.

questions.stem:
Consider the following functions from positive integers to real numbers:

$10,\ \sqrt{n},\ n,\ \log_2 n,\ \frac{100}{n}$.

The CORRECT arrangement of the above functions in increasing order of asymptotic complexity is:

steps.title: What asymptotic order means and the ladder to use
steps.body: $f$ is below $g$ asymptotically when $f(n)/g(n)\to0$ as $n$ grows; only large $n$ counts, and small values mislead. The ladder from slowest to fastest is: functions that shrink to 0, constants, logarithms, then powers $n^c$ in increasing order of $c$. The rule: place each function on the ladder and sort.

steps.title: Place each function
steps.body: $100/n$ shrinks to 0, so it is slowest of all. $10$ is a constant. $\log_2 n$ is unbounded, but slower than every positive power of $n$. $\sqrt n=n^{1/2}$. $n=n^1$. So the order is $100/n,\ 10,\ \log_2 n,\ \sqrt n,\ n$.

steps.title: Check with a large n
steps.body: At $n=2^{20}$ the values are about $0.0001,\ 10,\ 20,\ 1024,\ 1\,048\,576$, in that order, and the order stays the same at $2^{40}$ and $2^{80}$. At $n=1024$ we get $\log_2 n=10$, which ties with the constant; that is only the crossing point, and beyond it the logarithm is larger. This is option (B).

shortcut.body: Order by type: vanishing, constant, logarithm, root, linear. Confirm with $n=2^{20}$: $10^{-4},\ 10,\ 20,\ 1024,\ 10^6$. About 30 seconds.

traps.text: Putting $\log_2 n$ first because at small $n$ (for $n=2$ it is 1) it looks tiny. Asymptotics looks at large $n$, where $\log n$ passes 10 and $100/n$ is near 0.
Putting $\sqrt n$ below $\log_2 n$. Any positive power of $n$, even $n^{0.01}$, eventually exceeds $\log n$.
Putting the constant 10 above $\log_2 n$ after trying small $n$ (at $n=8$, $\log_2 n=3<10$). The logarithm reaches 10 at $n=1024$ and keeps growing, so it ends above the constant.

recognize.clues: Five functions to arrange in increasing asymptotic order, including a constant, a decaying term, a logarithm and powers of $n$. The words increasing asymptotic complexity point to the growth ladder.
recognize.contrast: The look-alike is comparing values at one small $n$, which can place the logarithm below the constant. Asymptotic order uses the limit as $n$ grows, not a single sample.

check.body: Use limits instead of sample values. $\frac{\log_2 n}{\sqrt n}\to0$, since the derivatives give $\frac{1/(n\ln 2)}{1/(2\sqrt n)}=\frac{2}{\ln2\,\sqrt n}\to0$, so the logarithm is below the root. $\frac{\sqrt n}{n}=\frac1{\sqrt n}\to0$ and $\frac{100/n}{10}=\frac{10}{n}\to0$. Also $\log_2 n\to\infty$ while $10$ stays fixed, so the constant is below the logarithm. Every adjacent pair is ordered as in option (B).

A function is below another when their ratio tends to 0. Any positive power of $n$, however small, eventually beats a logarithm, and a logarithm beats every constant.

questions.stem: Let $A$ be an array of 31 numbers consisting of a sequence of 0's followed by a sequence of 1's. The problem is to find the smallest index $i$ such that $A[i]$ is 1 by probing the minimum number of locations in $A$. The worst case number of probes performed by an optimal algorithm is ________.

solutionDiagram.alt: Bars of decreasing width showing the number of candidate answers left after each probe: 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1, so five probes are enough in the worst case.

steps.title: Probes, outcomes and the halving limit
steps.body: A probe reads one location $A[p]$ and sees 0 or 1. The array looks like $0\dots0\,1\dots1$, so the answer is the index $i$ of the first 1, and $A[p]=1$ exactly when $i\le p$. One probe therefore splits the possible answers into two groups, $i\le p$ and $i>p$. A probing strategy is a decision tree: each possible answer is a leaf, and a tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves. The rule: the worst-case number of probes is at least $\lceil\log_2(\text{number of possible answers})\rceil$, and splitting in halves reaches it.

steps.title: Count the possible answers
steps.body: The first 1 can be at index $1,2,\dots,31$, and the array could also be all 0s, which adds the outcome "no 1". That is 32 outcomes; if a 1 is guaranteed there are 31. Either way the lower bound is the same.

steps.title: Binary search reaches the bound
steps.body: Probe the middle, $A[16]$. If it is 1 the answer is among indices 1 to 16, else among 17 to 32: 16 candidates either way. Each probe halves the candidates: $32\to16\to8\to4\to2\to1$. That takes 5 probes, and the answer is then known without a further probe. A dynamic-programming search over every probing strategy on 31 cells confirms that 5 is the minimum. The answer is 5.

shortcut.body: Binary search on 31 cells needs $\lceil\log_2(31+1)\rceil=5$ probes. Check that 4 cannot work: 4 probes tell apart at most $2^4=16$ outcomes, fewer than 31. About 2 minutes.

traps.text: Answering 4 from $\lfloor\log_2 31\rfloor=4$. A floor undercounts: 4 probes give only $2^4=16$ leaves, fewer than the 31 or 32 outcomes, so a ceiling is needed.
Answering 31 or 16 by scanning from the left, or from the middle outwards, one location at a time. The 0s-then-1s order lets each probe discard half the array.
Answering 6 by adding a final probe to confirm the answer. After the fifth probe only one candidate remains, so no confirmation probe is needed.

recognize.clues: Zeros followed by ones, a single boundary to find, and the question asks for the minimum worst-case number of probes. The sorted two-valued structure allows halving.
recognize.contrast: Plain linear search treats cells as unrelated and may check all 31. The zeros-then-ones order lets each probe rule out half the cells, so the count is logarithmic.

check.body: Run the halving on the candidate count: each probe turns $k$ candidates into at most $\lceil k/2\rceil$, and the chain from 31 candidates ends at 1 after the same number of probes as the lower bound. Also check that one fewer probe fails: that many probes give only $2^4=16$ leaf outcomes, fewer than the 31 positions.

variation.stem: Let $A$ be an array of 100 numbers consisting of a sequence of 0s followed by a sequence of 1s, where the sequence of 1s may be empty. The problem is to find the smallest index $i$ such that $A[i]$ is 1, or to report that there is none, by probing the minimum number of locations. The worst-case number of probes performed by an optimal algorithm is ________.
variation.explanation: There are 101 outcomes: the first 1 at one of 100 positions, or no 1 at all. A decision tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves, and $2^6=64<101\le128=2^7$, so at least 7 probes are needed. Halving the candidates each time reaches this. A search over all strategies by program also gives 7.
